career_stage.notes: A demonstration consortium of €8–9 million with public authorities in several countries is not something an early-career lecturer would coordinate. Realistically you would join as a partner contributing modelling or digital-twin work.

data.recommend_reason: Only a small part of the topic is your science and you could not lead it; do not chase it, but say yes if a coordinator you trust offers a well-defined modelling or digital-twin work package.

data.recommend_reason: An open-topic grant you are fully eligible to lead, with no deadline; it is the obvious vehicle for your next substantial project after the New Investigator Award.

topic_fit.notes: Any field of research in EPSRC remit, so the visit serves your own programme, for example time at an overseas wave facility or with a scientific machine learning group. The case rests on why this visit, to this place, at this time.

career_stage.notes: Open to any EPSRC-eligible academic and built around one named project lead, so it is realistic for a new lecturer building international links. It is not reserved for early-career staff, but it is exactly the light travel and collaboration award you asked for.

eligibility.notes: EPSRC standard eligibility applies, which you meet as a permanent lecturer at an eligible UK research organisation. Only one person can be listed as project lead, and uninvited resubmissions are not accepted.

data.why_fit: It covers travel, subsistence, visas, your own salary time and indirect costs for a research visit, with no deadline and a two-page case, so it is a low-effort way to start an overseas collaboration. Well-supported applications can be funded without going to a panel, and a visit could seed a later joint bid through EPSRC's working with overseas scientists route.
data.concerns: No equipment (including laptops) or estates costs can be claimed, and you must show why the travel is necessary and alternatives would not do. Keep the visit distinct from travel already costed on your New Investigator Award, and agree the time away with your department.
data.recommend_reason: Open topic, light to apply for, always open and exactly the kind of travel and collaboration award you asked for.

career_stage.notes: Nothing bars a new lecturer, but assessors look for leadership and management skills and a group with a range of expertise and experience, which in practice favours a lead with established standing in the community. eligibility.notes: EPSRC standard eligibility rules apply, which you meet as a permanent academic at an eligible UK university. The network must be a new collaboration, and uninvited resubmissions are not accepted.

data.why_fit: The topic is open, and a focused community around scientific machine learning for waves and offshore engineering is something you could plausibly convene. Your experience as a CDT course director shows you can organise people across disciplines.
data.concerns: It funds meetings and coordination rather than research, and needs a heavy application (six-page case, costings, partner letters) followed by up to three years of organising — a poor trade while you are still building a group. data.recommend_reason: The topic is open, but leading a national network is a stretch at your stage and the scheme is neither light to apply for nor a source of research funding. Revisit it in a few years, or join a senior colleague's bid as the single co-lead.

data.recommend_reason: It fails both tests: the science is Arctic observing and marine autonomy rather than wave dynamics, and the single mission-scale award is aimed at established ocean-observing teams.

data.summary: An always-open route for a joint UK–US environmental science project that is reviewed once, with NERC funding the UK side at 80% FEC and NSF funding the US side. It is not a scheme of its own: you apply through NERC's Pushing the Frontiers or an NSF GEO or BIO programme, after both agencies approve an expression of interest.

topic_fit.notes: Any subject is allowed provided most of it lies within both NERC remit and an NSF GEO or BIO programme; for you that means NSF Ocean Sciences, with the project posed as ocean science (wave breaking, extreme sea states, coastal dynamics) and not as offshore engineering. There is no thematic steer.

career_stage.notes: Open to anyone who meets UKRI's individual eligibility rules, and you would lead only the UK side of a two-country project. The NSF-led option, with a UK component of up to £300,000, is a realistic scale for an early-career PI working with an established US partner.

eligibility.notes: You meet the UK rules as a lecturer at an organisation eligible for NERC funding, but you also need a US partner who is eligible for the relevant NSF programme. Both agencies check eligibility, remit and budget at the expression of interest and can reject it.

data.why_fit: If you have a US collaborator in ocean waves or physical oceanography, a single review removes the risk of one side being funded without the other, and the NSF-led option can bring you a UK component of up to £300,000 (at 100% FEC) with no second assessment by NERC. The route has no closing date of its own.
data.concerns: The science must fit both NERC and NSF GEO remits, which leaves out the engineering side of your work, and there are two stages on top of a full proposal. NERC asks you to read NSF's current priorities guidance first and warns that processing may take longer than usual; studentships cannot be requested, and NERC ship time is barred on NSF-led bids.
data.recommend_reason: Worth keeping in view if you have, or are building, a US partnership on an ocean-science question: open topic, a realistic UK role for an early-career PI and always open, but heavy and not for engineering-led projects.

data.summary: A standing agreement between UKRI and the Research Council of Norway that lets you add Norway-based co-leads to a UK-led application to an existing research council scheme, with their direct costs paid by UKRI. It is not a separate fund: it has no deadline or budget of its own, and the rules of the scheme you apply through still govern.

topic_fit.notes: Any discipline within the participating councils' remits qualifies, including EPSRC and NERC. Norway's strength in ocean waves and offshore engineering makes it a natural partner country for your work.

career_stage.notes: It rides on whichever scheme you apply to, so it is as realistic as that scheme: for you, most obviously an EPSRC standard research grant that you lead.

eligibility.notes: You qualify as a project lead employed by a UK research organisation eligible for EPSRC and NERC funding. The host opportunity must permit international co-leads; EPSRC's standard research grant explicitly allows a Norway-based one.

data.why_fit: It is a cost-free way to put real money behind a Norwegian collaboration: the co-lead's justified salary, locally employed researchers, travel and consumables can be paid at 100% of direct costs, up to 30% of the project's total. That suits your interest in light-touch international collaboration and would strengthen a wave or offshore-wind proposal you were writing anyway.
data.concerns: It only has value alongside a full application to another scheme, which is where the real effort and competition lie. Norwegian estates, overheads and indirect costs are not covered, no single item may cost more than £10,000, and Manchester must carry out due diligence and pass the funds on.
data.recommend_reason: Worth keeping in view because it adds a funded Norwegian partner to a grant you would lead anyway for almost no extra effort; treat it as an option on your next EPSRC or NERC application rather than a call in itself.
